Every block, documented reader ⇄ edit-canvas parity 26-agent audit

● FULL · 10 ◐ PARTIAL · 25 ○ VIEW-ONLY · 10
ELEMENTS
FULL · element · insertable. Fully editable — a paragraph is native contenteditable prose, every inline mark included, insertable via slash and Enter.
The most elemental block — meaning with nothing but its own text.

PARTIAL · element · not insertable. Fully editable in-canvas — click into the lede and type like a paragraph, marks and all; you just can't slash-insert one.

PARTIAL · element · not insertable. Quote text is fully editable inline with marks, but you can't insert a new pullquote from the canvas.

action — view vs edit

FULL · widget · insertable. Fully editable in-canvas: body text plus label and lead inputs all live-edit, and it's slash-insertable.
An annotated item: label + lead + body.

Code: note-node.js:58,138-158,215-246,254; islands :164-179; PM-hidden :261-272; lossy note :34-36

Terminal chrome wrapping child blocks.

PARTIAL · widget · insertable. Barely — you can edit the caption and nothing else; the figure's actual content is a read-only server-painted atom.

PARTIAL · widget · not insertable. Title and query-label edit live with server-bound rows, but you can't insert it and every other facet is raw-JSON only.
A live task query, rows resolved at read.
task-list — view vs edit

Fix: Add facet + config controls (project/status/parent selects, limit/fields select) and register it in CANVAS_SLASH_TYPES. Code: task-list-node.js:222-236, :329-384, :42-82, :153-155, :245-289; slash-insert.js:39-62

Choosing Your Site Framework

You're about to spawn a site on Barkpark Cloud — a live frontend that reads straight from your content. This guide exists so you can make that choice with open eyes: what each framework is genuinely good at, where it will bite you, and which one fits the site you actually want to ship. There is no single right answer — only the right answer *for your project*.

The short version. For most content sites — blogs, docs, marketing, portfolios — Astro is the best default, and it's the one you can spawn today. If you need a heavily interactive app, you'll want a server-rendered framework like Next.js or TanStack Start. Read on for why.

First, the decision that matters most

Before the framework, understand the axis every framework sits on. It decides your site's speed, cost, and how much can go wrong.

Static(pre-built pages)
Server-rendered(SSR)
What it isEvery page is built once into plain HTML/CSS/JSPages are assembled by a live server on each request
SpeedFastest possible — files served from the edgeFast, but every request does work
Cost & scaleEffectively free, scales infinitelyCosts grow with traffic; needs a running process
Best forContent that changes on a human scheduleContent that's personalised or changes per-request
What can breakAlmost nothing at runtimeThe server, under load or on bad input

Barkpark keeps your site and your content on the same wire — the site fetches from your Barkpark project over an internal connection, not the public internet. That means faster builds, private reads, and instant updates when your content changes. Static sites get this at build time; server-rendered sites get it on every request.

Why "close" matters here

  • Instant content updates — when you publish in Barkpark, your site knows immediately (no manual redeploy).
  • No rate limits, no egress fees — your site reads content over a private link, not a metered public API.
  • One login, one domain, one dashboard — the site inherits your workspace, project, and dataset scoping.
  • One deploy pipeline — updates roll out with zero downtime, the same way the rest of your Barkpark runs.

The frameworks in depth

Astro — the content-site flagship

Astro is built for exactly what a CMS produces: pages of content. It renders to static HTML by default and only ships JavaScript for the interactive "islands" you explicitly ask for. If you're building a blog, documentation site, marketing site, or portfolio, this is the one to reach for.

  • Not built for app-like UIs — if your site is mostly dashboards, live filtering, or complex client state, Astro's island model fights you.
  • Islands take a mental shift — sharing state between separate interactive components is deliberately awkward.
  • Smaller component ecosystem than the React/Next world.
  • Server-rendering is younger than Next's — battle-tested less at very large scale.

Recommended default, and spawnable today. If you're unsure, start here — you can always graduate to a heavier framework later.

Next.js — the do-everything heavyweight

Next.js is the most popular React framework and can build essentially any kind of site — from a static blog to a full SaaS app. That power comes with weight and complexity.

Best for: apps with logged-in users, dashboards, e-commerce, anything that mixes content with heavy interactivity.

Pros

  • Does everything — static pages, server-rendering, and incremental updates all in one framework.

  • Frequent breaking changes — major versions can mean real migration work.
  • Server-rendering costs more to run — dynamic pages need a live process, which grows with traffic.
  • Overkill for a brochure site — you'll carry complexity you never use.

TanStack Start — the modern, type-safe challenger

TanStack Start is a newer full-stack React framework built around the excellent TanStack Router. It prioritises end-to-end type safety and a fast, modern developer experience.

Best for: highly interactive, data-heavy applications where type safety and routing power matter.

Pros

  • End-to-end type safety — from your routes to your data, mistakes get caught before they ship.
  • Best-in-class routing — TanStack Router handles complex, nested, data-driven navigation elegantly.
  • Fast, modern tooling — built on Vite, so builds and hot-reload are quick.
  • Excellent for interactive apps — streaming server-rendering keeps data-heavy pages snappy.

Cons

  • Not content-first — overkill for a blog or marketing site.
  • Server-rendering runtime — same running-process cost as Next.
  • Fewer hireable specialists — a smaller talent pool than React/Next.
  • Younger = more risk — APIs are still settling compared to mature frameworks.

SvelteKit compiles your components away at build time, so the browser downloads very little framework code. It handles both static and server-rendered sites and is widely loved for its developer experience.

Best for: teams who want small, fast sites and enjoy a clean, minimal syntax — content or app.

Nuxt is to Vue what Next is to React: a mature, full-featured framework for building both content sites and applications. If your team knows Vue, this is the natural home.

Best for: Vue teams building content-rich sites or full applications.

Pros

  • Great content tooling — a dedicated content module makes CMS-driven sites straightforward.
  • Does static and server-rendering — flexible per page.
  • Approachable — Vue is often considered gentler to learn than React.

Cons

  • Smaller talent pool here than React-based options.
  • Server-rendering runtime cost identical to Next when you go SSR.
  • Ships more JS than an islands or compiled framework like Astro or Svelte.
  • Vue-only — you can't borrow the React component universe.

Hugo — the fastest static builder there is

Hugo is a single Go binary that turns content into a static site faster than anything else on this list. No Node.js, no runtime — just files. It's a superb fit for large content sites where build speed matters.

Best for: large blogs, documentation, and content sites where raw build speed and simplicity win.

Pros

  • Fastest builds on the market — thousands of pages in seconds.

Eleventy is a minimalist static site generator. It does very little on purpose, which makes it fast, predictable, and easy to reason about.

  • Smaller ecosystem than Astro or Next.

body.html:
Choosing Your Site Framework

You're about to spawn a site on Barkpark Cloud — a live frontend that reads straight from your content. This guide exists so you can make that choice with open eyes: what each framework is genuinely good at, where it will bite you, and which one fits the site you actually want to ship. There is no single right answer — only the right answer *for your project*.

The short version. For most content sites — blogs, docs, marketing, portfolios — Astro is the best default, and it's the one you can spawn today. If you need a heavily interactive app, you'll want a server-rendered framework like Next.js or TanStack Start. Read on for why.

First, the decision that matters most

Before the framework, understand the axis every framework sits on. It decides your site's speed, cost, and how much can go wrong.

Static (pre-built pages)Server-rendered (SSR)
What it isEvery page is built once into plain HTML/CSS/JSPages are assembled by a live server on each request
SpeedFastest possible — files served from the edgeFast, but every request does work
Cost & scaleEffectively free, scales infinitelyCosts grow with traffic; needs a running process
Best forContent that changes on a human scheduleContent that's personalised or changes per-request
What can breakAlmost nothing at runtimeThe server, under load or on bad input

Barkpark keeps your site and your content on the same wire — the site fetches from your Barkpark project over an internal connection, not the public internet. That means faster builds, private reads, and instant updates when your content changes. Static sites get this at build time; server-rendered sites get it on every request.

Why "close" matters here

• Instant content updates — when you publish in Barkpark, your site knows immediately (no manual redeploy).
• No rate limits, no egress fees — your site reads content over a private link, not a metered public API.
• One login, one domain, one dashboard — the site inherits your workspace, project, and dataset scoping.
• One deploy pipeline — updates roll out with zero downtime, the same way the rest of your Barkpark runs.

The frameworks at a glance

FrameworkLanguageBest atRuntimeShips JS by defaultOn Barkpark Cloud
AstroJS / TSContent sitesStatic or SSRAlmost noneAvailable now
Next.jsJS / TSEverythingStatic or SSRA lotComing
TanStack StartJS / TSInteractive appsSSRA lotComing
SvelteKitJS / TSBothStatic or SSRVery littleComing
NuxtJS / TS (Vue)Content + appStatic or SSRModerateComing
HugoGoContent sitesStatic onlyNoneComing
EleventyJSSimple contentStatic onlyNoneComing
Barkpark Native—Instant sitesRendered for youNoneAvailable now
"Ships JS by default" is a proxy for page weight and speed. Less shipped JavaScript means faster loads and better search rankings — which is why content-first frameworks win on SEO.

The frameworks in depth

Astro — the content-site flagship

Astro is built for exactly what a CMS produces: pages of content. It renders to static HTML by default and only ships JavaScript for the interactive "islands" you explicitly ask for. If you're building a blog, documentation site, marketing site, or portfolio, this is the one to reach for.

Best for: blogs, docs, marketing sites, portfolios, landing pages, changelogs.

Pros

• Blazing fast by design — ships near-zero JavaScript, so pages load instantly and score top marks on Core Web Vitals.
• Built for headless CMS — its content layer is designed to pull from an external source like Barkpark, so the integration is natural, not bolted on.
• Excellent SEO out of the box — fast, static, semantic HTML is what search engines reward.
• Use any UI library — drop in React, Svelte, Vue, or Solid components as islands; you're not locked into one.
• Gentle learning curve — if you know HTML and a little JS, you can be productive in an afternoon.
• Cheapest to host — static output means your site is basically free to serve and scales without limit.
• Grows with you — start static, add server-rendering later for the few pages that need it.
• Huge, active ecosystem of themes and integrations to start from.

Cons

• Not built for app-like UIs — if your site is mostly dashboards, live filtering, or complex client state, Astro's island model fights you.
• Islands take a mental shift — sharing state between separate interactive components is deliberately awkward.
• Smaller component ecosystem than the React/Next world.
• Server-rendering is younger than Next's — battle-tested less at very large scale.
Recommended default, and spawnable today. If you're unsure, start here — you can always graduate to a heavier framework later.

Next.js — the do-everything heavyweight

Next.js is the most popular React framework and can build essentially any kind of site — from a static blog to a full SaaS app. That power comes with weight and complexity.

Best for: apps with logged-in users, dashboards, e-commerce, anything that mixes content with heavy interactivity.

Pros

• Does everything — static pages, server-rendering, and incremental updates all in one framework.
• The largest ecosystem — the most tutorials, templates, integrations, and hireable developers of any framework here.
• Great for interactive apps — if your site has accounts, carts, or dashboards, Next is at home.
• Incremental Static Regeneration — pages can rebuild in the background as content changes, blending static speed with fresh data.
• First-class React — access to the entire React component universe.

Cons

• Heavy — ships a lot of JavaScript, so pages are slower than a static Astro or Hugo site unless carefully tuned.
• Complex — React Server Components and the App Router have a real learning curve, and the "right way" keeps evolving.
• Frequent breaking changes — major versions can mean real migration work.
• Server-rendering costs more to run — dynamic pages need a live process, which grows with traffic.
• Overkill for a brochure site — you'll carry complexity you never use.

TanStack Start — the modern, type-safe challenger

TanStack Start is a newer full-stack React framework built around the excellent TanStack Router. It prioritises end-to-end type safety and a fast, modern developer experience.

Best for: highly interactive, data-heavy applications where type safety and routing power matter.

Pros

• End-to-end type safety — from your routes to your data, mistakes get caught before they ship.
• Best-in-class routing — TanStack Router handles complex, nested, data-driven navigation elegantly.
• Fast, modern tooling — built on Vite, so builds and hot-reload are quick.
• Excellent for interactive apps — streaming server-rendering keeps data-heavy pages snappy.

Cons

• The newest option here — smaller community, fewer templates, fewer answers when you hit a wall.
• Not content-first — overkill for a blog or marketing site.
• Server-rendering runtime — same running-process cost as Next.
• Fewer hireable specialists — a smaller talent pool than React/Next.
• Younger = more risk — APIs are still settling compared to mature frameworks.

SvelteKit — small, fast, and pleasant

SvelteKit compiles your components away at build time, so the browser downloads very little framework code. It handles both static and server-rendered sites and is widely loved for its developer experience.

Best for: teams who want small, fast sites and enjoy a clean, minimal syntax — content or app.

Pros

• Tiny bundles — the framework compiles itself out, so pages are light and fast.
• Loved developer experience — concise syntax, less boilerplate than React.
• Flexible — does static and server-rendering equally well.
• Built-in essentials — routing, data loading, and forms come in the box.

Cons

• Smaller ecosystem than React — fewer ready-made components and integrations.
• Fewer Svelte developers to hire than React developers.
• Server-rendering runtime cost when you choose SSR.
• Less enterprise track record than Next at very large scale.

Nuxt — the Vue powerhouse

Nuxt is to Vue what Next is to React: a mature, full-featured framework for building both content sites and applications. If your team knows Vue, this is the natural home.

Best for: Vue teams building content-rich sites or full applications.

Pros

• Mature and complete — years of production use, batteries included.
• Great content tooling — a dedicated content module makes CMS-driven sites straightforward.
• Does static and server-rendering — flexible per page.
• Approachable — Vue is often considered gentler to learn than React.

Cons

• Smaller talent pool here than React-based options.
• Server-rendering runtime cost identical to Next when you go SSR.
• Ships more JS than an islands or compiled framework like Astro or Svelte.
• Vue-only — you can't borrow the React component universe.

Hugo — the fastest static builder there is

Hugo is a single Go binary that turns content into a static site faster than anything else on this list. No Node.js, no runtime — just files. It's a superb fit for large content sites where build speed matters.

Best for: large blogs, documentation, and content sites where raw build speed and simplicity win.

Pros

• Fastest builds on the market — thousands of pages in seconds.
• No JavaScript runtime needed — a single binary, nothing to keep alive, nothing to patch.
• Cheapest and safest to host — pure static output, no server code to attack.
• Massive theme library — hundreds of ready-made designs.
• Rock-solid and stable — mature, with few breaking changes.

Cons

• Weak on interactivity — no built-in "islands" story; dynamic bits need hand-rolled JavaScript.
• Go templates are clunkier than modern component syntax.
• Not for app-like sites — static only, by design.
• Smaller front-end developer familiarity than the JavaScript frameworks.

Eleventy (11ty) — dead-simple static

Eleventy is a minimalist static site generator. It does very little on purpose, which makes it fast, predictable, and easy to reason about.

Best for: simple content sites where you want maximum control and minimum magic.

Pros

• Extremely simple — little to learn, little to go wrong.
• Zero JavaScript shipped — pages are as light as they get.
• Fast builds and a tiny footprint.
• Template-language freedom — write pages in whichever templating style you like.

Cons

• No interactivity story — you add all dynamic behaviour yourself.
• Very hands-on — the minimalism means more wiring for anything non-trivial.
• Smaller ecosystem than Astro or Next.
• Static only — no server-rendering path.

Barkpark Native — the instant, zero-effort site

Not every site needs a framework. Barkpark can render your content as a live site directly — no build step, no code, no framework to learn. Publish content, get a site. It's the fastest way from "I have content" to "it's online."

Best for: getting content live in seconds, previews, and anyone who doesn't want to touch a framework at all.

Pros

• Instant — live in seconds, with nothing to build or deploy.
• Zero code and zero maintenance — Barkpark handles the rendering and the updates.

preimage.body_html:
Choosing Your Site Framework

You're about to spawn a site on Barkpark Cloud — a live frontend that reads straight from your content. This guide exists so you can make that choice with open eyes: what each framework is genuinely good at, where it will bite you, and which one fits the site you actually want to ship. There is no single right answer — only the right answer *for your project*.

The short version. For most content sites — blogs, docs, marketing, portfolios — Astro is the best default, and it's the one you can spawn today. If you need a heavily interactive app, you'll want a server-rendered framework like Next.js or TanStack Start. Read on for why.

First, the decision that matters most

Before the framework, understand the axis every framework sits on. It decides your site's speed, cost, and how much can go wrong.

Static (pre-built pages)Server-rendered (SSR)
What it isEvery page is built once into plain HTML/CSS/JSPages are assembled by a live server on each request
SpeedFastest possible — files served from the edgeFast, but every request does work
Cost & scaleEffectively free, scales infinitelyCosts grow with traffic; needs a running process
Best forContent that changes on a human scheduleContent that's personalised or changes per-request
What can breakAlmost nothing at runtimeThe server, under load or on bad input

Barkpark keeps your site and your content on the same wire — the site fetches from your Barkpark project over an internal connection, not the public internet. That means faster builds, private reads, and instant updates when your content changes. Static sites get this at build time; server-rendered sites get it on every request.

Why "close" matters here

  • Instant content updates — when you publish in Barkpark, your site knows immediately (no manual redeploy).
  • No rate limits, no egress fees — your site reads content over a private link, not a metered public API.
  • One login, one domain, one dashboard — the site inherits your workspace, project, and dataset scoping.
  • One deploy pipeline — updates roll out with zero downtime, the same way the rest of your Barkpark runs.
§

The frameworks at a glance

FrameworkLanguageBest atRuntimeShips JS by defaultOn Barkpark Cloud
AstroJS / TSContent sitesStatic or SSRAlmost noneAvailable now
Next.jsJS / TSEverythingStatic or SSRA lotComing
TanStack StartJS / TSInteractive appsSSRA lotComing
SvelteKitJS / TSBothStatic or SSRVery littleComing
NuxtJS / TS (Vue)Content + appStatic or SSRModerateComing
HugoGoContent sitesStatic onlyNoneComing
EleventyJSSimple contentStatic onlyNoneComing
Barkpark Native—Instant sitesRendered for youNoneAvailable now
"Ships JS by default" is a proxy for page weight and speed. Less shipped JavaScript means faster loads and better search rankings — which is why content-first frameworks win on SEO.
§

The frameworks in depth

Astro — the content-site flagship

Astro is built for exactly what a CMS produces: pages of content. It renders to static HTML by default and only ships JavaScript for the interactive "islands" you explicitly ask for. If you're building a blog, documentation site, marketing site, or portfolio, this is the one to reach for.

Best for: blogs, docs, marketing sites, portfolios, landing pages, changelogs.

Pros

  • Blazing fast by design — ships near-zero JavaScript, so pages load instantly and score top marks on Core Web Vitals.
  • Built for headless CMS — its content layer is designed to pull from an external source like Barkpark, so the integration is natural, not bolted on.
  • Excellent SEO out of the box — fast, static, semantic HTML is what search engines reward.
  • Use any UI library — drop in React, Svelte, Vue, or Solid components as islands; you're not locked into one.
  • Gentle learning curve — if you know HTML and a little JS, you can be productive in an afternoon.
  • Cheapest to host — static output means your site is basically free to serve and scales without limit.
  • Grows with you — start static, add server-rendering later for the few pages that need it.
  • Huge, active ecosystem of themes and integrations to start from.

Cons

  • Not built for app-like UIs — if your site is mostly dashboards, live filtering, or complex client state, Astro's island model fights you.
  • Islands take a mental shift — sharing state between separate interactive components is deliberately awkward.
  • Smaller component ecosystem than the React/Next world.
  • Server-rendering is younger than Next's — battle-tested less at very large scale.
Recommended default, and spawnable today. If you're unsure, start here — you can always graduate to a heavier framework later.

Next.js — the do-everything heavyweight

Next.js is the most popular React framework and can build essentially any kind of site — from a static blog to a full SaaS app. That power comes with weight and complexity.

Best for: apps with logged-in users, dashboards, e-commerce, anything that mixes content with heavy interactivity.

Pros

  • Does everything — static pages, server-rendering, and incremental updates all in one framework.
  • The largest ecosystem — the most tutorials, templates, integrations, and hireable developers of any framework here.
  • Great for interactive apps — if your site has accounts, carts, or dashboards, Next is at home.
  • Incremental Static Regeneration — pages can rebuild in the background as content changes, blending static speed with fresh data.
  • First-class React — access to the entire React component universe.

Cons

  • Heavy — ships a lot of JavaScript, so pages are slower than a static Astro or Hugo site unless carefully tuned.
  • Complex — React Server Components and the App Router have a real learning curve, and the "right way" keeps evolving.
  • Frequent breaking changes — major versions can mean real migration work.
  • Server-rendering costs more to run — dynamic pages need a live process, which grows with traffic.
  • Overkill for a brochure site — you'll carry complexity you never use.

TanStack Start — the modern, type-safe challenger

TanStack Start is a newer full-stack React framework built around the excellent TanStack Router. It prioritises end-to-end type safety and a fast, modern developer experience.

Best for: highly interactive, data-heavy applications where type safety and routing power matter.

Pros

  • End-to-end type safety — from your routes to your data, mistakes get caught before they ship.
  • Best-in-class routing — TanStack Router handles complex, nested, data-driven navigation elegantly.
  • Fast, modern tooling — built on Vite, so builds and hot-reload are quick.
  • Excellent for interactive apps — streaming server-rendering keeps data-heavy pages snappy.

Cons

  • The newest option here — smaller community, fewer templates, fewer answers when you hit a wall.
  • Not content-first — overkill for a blog or marketing site.
  • Server-rendering runtime — same running-process cost as Next.
  • Fewer hireable specialists — a smaller talent pool than React/Next.
  • Younger = more risk — APIs are still settling compared to mature frameworks.

SvelteKit — small, fast, and pleasant

SvelteKit compiles your components away at build time, so the browser downloads very little framework code. It handles both static and server-rendered sites and is widely loved for its developer experience.

Best for: teams who want small, fast sites and enjoy a clean, minimal syntax — content or app.

Pros

  • Tiny bundles — the framework compiles itself out, so pages are light and fast.
  • Loved developer experience — concise syntax, less boilerplate than React.
  • Flexible — does static and server-rendering equally well.
  • Built-in essentials — routing, data loading, and forms come in the box.

Cons

  • Smaller ecosystem than React — fewer ready-made components and integrations.
  • Fewer Svelte developers to hire than React developers.
  • Server-rendering runtime cost when you choose SSR.
  • Less enterprise track record than Next at very large scale.

Nuxt — the Vue powerhouse

Nuxt is to Vue what Next is to React: a mature, full-featured framework for building both content sites and applications. If your team knows Vue, this is the natural home.

Best for: Vue teams building content-rich sites or full applications.

Pros

  • Mature and complete — years of production use, batteries included.
  • Great content tooling — a dedicated content module makes CMS-driven sites straightforward.
  • Does static and server-rendering — flexible per page.
  • Approachable — Vue is often considered gentler to learn than React.

Cons

  • Smaller talent pool here than React-based options.
  • Server-rendering runtime cost identical to Next when you go SSR.
  • Ships more JS than an islands or compiled framework like Astro or Svelte.
  • Vue-only — you can't borrow the React component universe.

Hugo — the fastest static builder there is

Hugo is a single Go binary that turns content into a static site faster than anything else on this list. No Node.js, no runtime — just files. It's a superb fit for large content sites where build speed matters.

Best for: large blogs, documentation, and content sites where raw build speed and simplicity win.

Pros

  • Fastest builds on the market — thousands of pages in seconds.
  • No JavaScript runtime needed — a single binary, nothing to keep alive, nothing to patch.
  • Cheapest and safest to host — pure static output, no server code to attack.
  • Massive theme library — hundreds of ready-made designs.
  • Rock-solid and stable — mature, with few breaking changes.

Cons

  • Weak on interactivity — no built-in "islands" story; dynamic bits need hand-rolled JavaScript.
  • Go templates are clunkier than modern component syntax.
  • Not for app-like sites — static only, by design.
  • Smaller front-end developer familiarity than the JavaScript frameworks.

Eleventy (11ty) — dead-simple static

Eleventy is a minimalist static site generator. It does very little on purpose, which makes it fast, predictable, and easy to reason about.

Best for: simple content sites where you want maximum control and minimum magic.

Pros

  • Extremely simple — little to learn, little to go wrong.
  • Zero JavaScript shipped — pages are as light as they get.
  • Fast builds and a tiny footprint.
  • Template-language freedom — write pages in whichever templating style you like.

Cons

  • No interactivity story — you add all dynamic behaviour yourself.
  • Very hands-on — the minimalism means more wiring for anything non-trivial.
  • Smaller ecosystem than Astro or Next.
  • Static only — no server-rendering path.

Barkpark Native — the instant, zero-effort site

Not every site needs a framework. Barkpark can render your content as a live site directly — no build step, no code, no framework to learn. Publish content, get a site. It's the fastest way from "I have content" to "it's online."

Best for: getting content live in seconds, previews, and anyone who doesn't want to touch a framework at all.

Pros

  • Instant — live in seconds, with nothing to build or deploy.
  • Zero code and zero maintenance — Barkpark handles the rendering and the updates.
  • Always in sync — the site *is* your content; there's no separate copy to fall out of date.
  • No runtime to pay for or secure — it runs on infrastructure you already have.

Cons

  • Barkpark's look, not yours — you theme within what Barkpark offers, rather than designing freely.
  • Not for bespoke designs — if you need pixel-level custom layouts, reach for a framework.
  • Limited custom interactivity — it's a content site, not an app platform.
Available today. The zero-friction way to get online while you decide whether you need a full framework.

blocks.text: The Wave Deck — the epic cycle as an interactive, slide-by-slide experience

content.value: One wave, one deck 5 decision gates Live fleet, live ledger

The 7-phase epic cycle already externalizes everything it knows into Barkpark — a living wave Paper, a published task ledger, a wave_status heartbeat. The Wave Deck renders that state as slides a human can ride: watch the fleet fly in realtime, see exactly what was checked and what wasn't, and DECIDE at five gates whether to research more, build, or land. This paper is the information spec: slide by slide, what each screen must inform, what is live, where the data already lives, and what is genuinely open for design.

What this paper is (and isn't) This is the what-to-inform spec for Claude design — content, data sources, decision moments, live elements. It deliberately says nothing about visual style, layout, or component aesthetics. Every slide below states its job in one line; if a slide can't, it shouldn't exist.
Job: one glance answers “where is the wave, and how many minds are on it right now?” The current phase is lit; every gate shows whether it's upcoming, open (waiting on the user), or passed.
The cycle with its five user gates. Every ↺ edge is a deliberate, cheap loop — research costs Sonnet minutes, not Opus hours.
4 thinking phases (1 Fable each) 5–20 survey fleet ≤15 verify fleet ≤8 build fleet 5 user gates
Must inform: current phase · live agent count (flying / done / stalled) · elapsed time per phase vs its budget (~5 min, ~5 min, ~10 min, open) · which gate comes next and what will be decided there.

Data: phase + fleet counts from the workflow run (phase groups, agent labels); position also mirrored in the epic task's wave_status heartbeat (“wave: surveying — …”), so the deck can render from bp alone even after the run ends.
Job: the wave at a glance — for someone who just walked in.

items: The wish, verbatim. It is the focus of every phase; the deck leads with it, always visible (persistent header or recurring element).
Epic + wave identity: epic task id, wave Paper id, charter path, date.
Live status line: the wave_status heartbeat, rendered as state — surveying / verifying / building 6 slices / complete, grade B+.
Outcome when closed: grade with its one-line commentary hook — never a bare number (Cody mandate).

content.value: Data: bp task get <epic> → wave_status , wave_paper ; the Paper's title block.
Job: show the bet before the evidence — what the strategist thinks the finished experience is, and what it wants scouted.

items: Direction statement — the bold hypothesis, marked clearly as tentative (“Decide finalizes after two explore rounds”).
The survey plan — every question with its why (“how the answer changes the plan”). This is the first place the user can intervene: a wrong question at minute 5 is the cheapest bug in the whole cycle.
Soft gate — “fly the survey (N Sonnets)” is the default with a short countdown; the user can add/strike questions or annotate the direction before launch. Auto mode skips the pause entirely.

content.value: Data: wave Paper §Strategize (direction + survey plan land there before the fleet flies).

Job: the realtime spectacle with substance — you SEE 5–20 minds working, and each one is inspectable. This is where the deck rides the existing Studio chat surface: the wave is a chat session; the fleet is the agents rail; clicking an agent is the drill-down.
Per-agent card (the unit of this slide):

items: assignment key + the question, one line ( survey:auth-seams )
model tier badge (Sonnet/Opus/Fable) — the user asked to SEE the amount and kind of agents; make the fleet composition legible at a glance
state: queued · flying · reporting · done · died (agents can die on API errors — show it honestly, with what was lost)
live activity: elapsed time, files touched so far, last action line (streamed from the agent transcript — the chat feature already streams this)
on done: found/not-found/partial counts from its coverage[] — the card flips from activity to result

content.value: Realtime contract Liveness comes from two independent feeds and the deck must survive either going quiet: (1) the chat/workflow stream — agent spawn, phase change, tool activity, tokens; (2) the bp ledger — heartbeat, task stamps, Paper sections, which persist. Stream dies → deck degrades to polling bp and says so. Never render a frozen “live” view as if it were current.
Data: workflow phase groups + agent labels (spawn/complete events); Studio chat SESSIONS surface (agents rail, per-agent drill-down transcripts); tokens/elapsed from the run.

Job: make the EDGES of knowledge visible — this slide is the honest heart of the deck and the evidence base for Gate 1. Not “what did we learn” but “what did we check, what did we find, what did we check and NOT find, and where did nobody look”.

items: Checked & found — path, what it was checked for, the one-line takeaway.
Checked & NOT found — rendered as loudly as found. “No existing rate limiter in api/” is a decision-in-waiting, not a footnote.
Partial — ran out of timebox; candidates for the verify round.
Unreached corners — named by the Digest; unlisted = unchecked is the rule, so the map must admit its own blank space.
Open questions — every surveyor's parked unknowns, deduped.

content.value: Aggregations that matter: N files checked across M surveyors · found/not-found/partial ratio · which repo areas got zero coverage. A heatmap over repo areas is a natural fit; the raw per-file table must stay one tap away — trust comes from the ability to drill to the specific file and claim.
Data: surveyors' structured coverage[] ({path, checked_for, found|not_found|partial, note}), folded into wave Paper §Survey digest by the Digest phase.
Job: the Digest Fable's synthesis, contradictions named, and the proposed verify fleet — then the wave STOPS and asks. This is the user's “research more?” moment and the reason the deck exists.
Must inform before the user can decide:

items: what is now established (with the coverage map one slide back)
where survey reports contradict each other or the direction — verbatim, both sides
what remains unknown that Decide cannot live without — the justification for every verify assignment
the proposed verify fleet: per assignment its question, model (Sonnet vs Opus — and why the expensive one, when chosen ), and what will be RUN as proof vs merely read
cost of each option: another survey round ≈ N Sonnet-minutes; the verify round ≈ this fleet; skipping ahead ≈ deciding on unproven claims (name which)

content.value: Add or edit survey questions (user can type their own); another cheap Sonnet round flies; the Paper and coverage map grow — never fork. papers.derived_html:
Epic cycle · design handoff spec

The Wave Deck — the epic cycle as an interactive, slide-by-slide experience

One wave, one deck 5 decision gates Live fleet, live ledger

The 7-phase epic cycle already externalizes everything it knows into Barkpark — a living wave Paper, a published task ledger, a wave_status heartbeat. The Wave Deck renders that state as slides a human can ride: watch the fleet fly in realtime, see exactly what was checked and what wasn't, and DECIDE at five gates whether to research more, build, or land. This paper is the information spec: slide by slide, what each screen must inform, what is live, where the data already lives, and what is genuinely open for design.

What this paper is (and isn't) This is the what-to-inform spec for Claude design — content, data sources, decision moments, live elements. It deliberately says nothing about visual style, layout, or component aesthetics. Every slide below states its job in one line; if a slide can't, it shouldn't exist.

Slide 0 — The Loop (orientation map)

Job: one glance answers “where is the wave, and how many minds are on it right now?” The current phase is lit; every gate shows whether it's upcoming, open (waiting on the user), or passed.

The cycle with its five user gates. Every ↺ edge is a deliberate, cheap loop — research costs Sonnet minutes, not Opus hours.

4 thinking phases (1 Fable each) 5–20 survey fleet ≤15 verify fleet ≤8 build fleet 5 user gates

Must inform: current phase · live agent count (flying / done / stalled) · elapsed time per phase vs its budget (~5 min, ~5 min, ~10 min, open) · which gate comes next and what will be decided there.

Data: phase + fleet counts from the workflow run (phase groups, agent labels); position also mirrored in the epic task's wave_status heartbeat (“wave: surveying — …”), so the deck can render from bp alone even after the run ends.

Slide 1 — The Wave Card (cover)

Job: the wave at a glance — for someone who just walked in.

  • The wish, verbatim. It is the focus of every phase; the deck leads with it, always visible (persistent header or recurring element).
  • Epic + wave identity: epic task id, wave Paper id, charter path, date.
  • Live status line: the wave_status heartbeat, rendered as state — surveying / verifying / building 6 slices / complete, grade B+.
  • Outcome when closed: grade with its one-line commentary hook — never a bare number (Cody mandate).

Data: bp task get <epic> → wave_status , wave_paper ; the Paper's title block.

Slide 2 — Direction (Strategize)

Job: show the bet before the evidence — what the strategist thinks the finished experience is, and what it wants scouted.

  • Direction statement — the bold hypothesis, marked clearly as tentative (“Decide finalizes after two explore rounds”).
  • The survey plan — every question with its why (“how the answer changes the plan”). This is the first place the user can intervene: a wrong question at minute 5 is the cheapest bug in the whole cycle.
  • Soft gate — “fly the survey (N Sonnets)” is the default with a short countdown; the user can add/strike questions or annotate the direction before launch. Auto mode skips the pause entirely.

Data: wave Paper §Strategize (direction + survey plan land there before the fleet flies).

Slide 3 — Fleet in Flight (Survey, live)

Job: the realtime spectacle with substance — you SEE 5–20 minds working, and each one is inspectable. This is where the deck rides the existing Studio chat surface: the wave is a chat session; the fleet is the agents rail; clicking an agent is the drill-down.

Per-agent card (the unit of this slide):

  • assignment key + the question, one line ( survey:auth-seams )
  • model tier badge (Sonnet/Opus/Fable) — the user asked to SEE the amount and kind of agents; make the fleet composition legible at a glance
  • state: queued · flying · reporting · done · died (agents can die on API errors — show it honestly, with what was lost)
  • live activity: elapsed time, files touched so far, last action line (streamed from the agent transcript — the chat feature already streams this)
  • on done: found/not-found/partial counts from its coverage[] — the card flips from activity to result

Realtime contract Liveness comes from two independent feeds and the deck must survive either going quiet: (1) the chat/workflow stream — agent spawn, phase change, tool activity, tokens; (2) the bp ledger — heartbeat, task stamps, Paper sections, which persist. Stream dies → deck degrades to polling bp and says so. Never render a frozen “live” view as if it were current.

Data: workflow phase groups + agent labels (spawn/complete events); Studio chat SESSIONS surface (agents rail, per-agent drill-down transcripts); tokens/elapsed from the run.

Slide 4 — The Coverage Map (Survey results)

Job: make the EDGES of knowledge visible — this slide is the honest heart of the deck and the evidence base for Gate 1. Not “what did we learn” but “what did we check, what did we find, what did we check and NOT find, and where did nobody look”.

  • Checked & found — path, what it was checked for, the one-line takeaway.
  • Checked & NOT found — rendered as loudly as found. “No existing rate limiter in api/” is a decision-in-waiting, not a footnote.
  • Partial — ran out of timebox; candidates for the verify round.
  • Unreached corners — named by the Digest; unlisted = unchecked is the rule, so the map must admit its own blank space.
  • Open questions — every surveyor's parked unknowns, deduped.

Aggregations that matter: N files checked across M surveyors · found/not-found/partial ratio · which repo areas got zero coverage. A heatmap over repo areas is a natural fit; the raw per-file table must stay one tap away — trust comes from the ability to drill to the specific file and claim.

Data: surveyors' structured coverage[] ({path, checked_for, found|not_found|partial, note}), folded into wave Paper §Survey digest by the Digest phase.

Slide 5 — Synthesis & GATE 1: enough ground?

Job: the Digest Fable's synthesis, contradictions named, and the proposed verify fleet — then the wave STOPS and asks. This is the user's “research more?” moment and the reason the deck exists.

Must inform before the user can decide:

  • what is now established (with the coverage map one slide back)
  • where survey reports contradict each other or the direction — verbatim, both sides
  • what remains unknown that Decide cannot live without — the justification for every verify assignment
  • the proposed verify fleet: per assignment its question, model (Sonnet vs Opus — and why the expensive one, when chosen ), and what will be RUN as proof vs merely read
  • cost of each option: another survey round ≈ N Sonnet-minutes; the verify round ≈ this fleet; skipping ahead ≈ deciding on unproven claims (name which)

Add or edit survey questions (user can type their own); another cheap Sonnet round flies; the Paper and coverage map grow — never fork. Research more ↺ Approve the fleet as designed (default). User may strike or add assignments and flip a Sonnet↔Opus choice before launch. Verify → “I already know enough.” Deck names the claims that will go unproven; the choice is logged into the Paper with a dated note. Skip ahead ⏩

Data: wave Paper §Survey digest + §Verify plan (written BEFORE the fleet flies — the Paper always states what is in flight); gate choice appends a dated decision note to the Paper.

Slide 6 — Proof Runs (Verify, live)

Job: same fleet view as Slide 3, but the cards are proof-oriented: which command is running, live output tail, pass/fail as it lands. Mixed fleet — the Sonnet/Opus badges now carry meaning the user chose at Gate 1.

$ verify:search-seal — RUNNING CC=/usr/bin/clang mix test test/barkpark/access/grant_search_deny_test.exs ... 1 test, 1 failure ← RED: the leak is REAL (repro proves the hole)

Data: agent transcripts (chat drill-down) for live tails; structured proofs[] ({claim, command, output_excerpt, passed}) on completion.

Slide 7 — The Proof Table & GATE 2: proven enough?

Job: every load-bearing claim with its verdict and the actual output that earned it. Refuted premises get top billing — a premise that died here just saved a build slice.

  • proof rows: claim → command → decisive output excerpt → PROVEN / REFUTED — the excerpt is mandatory (distrust vacuous green: a pass only counts if the right thing produced it)
  • claims that arrived unproven (assignment had no runnable proof) — flagged, not hidden
  • verifier coverage delta — what the deep round checked that the survey hadn't

Target the still-unproven claims; user can demand a specific proof (“run the deny repro against X”). Verify more ↺ Default when every load-bearing claim is proven or consciously accepted as unproven (logged). Proceed to Decide →

Data: wave Paper §Verification results (Decide writes it) + workflow return proofs count; per-claim rows from verifiers' structured output.

Slide 8 — The Plan & GATE 3: approve the wave

Job: the biggest decision on the deck: exactly what will be built, by which class of mind, proven by what. Nothing here is hypothetical — every slice IS a published bp task the user can open.

  • Decisions — each with its one-line why; where verification overturned the original direction, show the reversal explicitly (before → after).
  • Slice cards = task cards: title · bp task id (live link) · surface · builder model badge (Opus = well-specified; Fable = subtle/high-blast-radius — the badge carries the architect's reasoning on hover/tap) · the exact gate command · acceptance criteria with their merge-gated ones marked.
  • Backlog seeded — discovered-but-deferred tasks filed now; the ledger shows the future, render it.
  • Fleet preview — N builders about to fly, model mix, expected file-overlap = zero (slices are worktree-isolated by design).

Fire the builders (default). The Paper already carries the plan; the heartbeat flips to “building N slices”. Build → Strike slices (their tasks stay filed, unclaimed, honest in the backlog) or demote/promote a builder model; then fire. Trim / retarget The plan is wrong at the root — send it back to Digest with a note. Expensive and rare; the note becomes lead_notes for the re-run. Redirect ↺

Data: wave Paper §Decisions + §Wave plan; slice tasks live via task-board query on parent_id=<epic> — this block type already exists in PortableDoc and renders the published ledger.

Slide 9 — The Build Board (live)

Job: the long phase, made watchable. The ledger's stamp-as-you-go contract means the board moves the moment reality does — criteria flip with evidence attached, stalls surface with the builder's own note, nothing waits for the end of the run.

  • per-slice: claim state (claimed by whom, when) → criteria flipping live, each with its evidence snippet → gate status (running/red/green) → branch + commit when done
  • stall = first-class state: the builder stamps why (“gate red on X, investigating”) — the card shows it the moment it's stamped, not at post-mortem
  • fleet strip: same per-agent cards as Slide 3 (builders now, model badges meaningful), drill-down into any builder's transcript mid-build

Data: published task ledger (criteria[], claim, lifecycle) — poll or realtime via the existing webhook/LiveView channel; agent stream for transcripts. The deck needs NO new write path: builders already stamp everything.

Slide 10 — The Verdict & GATE 4: land it?

Job: the reviewer's honest account, slice by slice, then the wave's grade — and the user's call on landing.

  • per slice: what the reviewer FIXED in place (or “none”) · final branch (-r if touched) · gate re-run result · the honest verdict incl. what the lead must know before merging
  • cross-slice coherence findings; ledger audit outcome (were the builders' live stamps truthful?)
  • The grade with its commentary — the commentary EARNS the grade; render them as one unit, never a bare letter (Cody mandate)
  • what stalled and why, with its honest task state

Merge the final branches; the lead closes merge-gated criteria on merge — the deck lists exactly which ones per slice. Land → Named issues go back to build — as bp tasks, so the loop stays in the ledger. Fix round ↺ Branches stay, tasks stay in_progress with honest notes; the debrief records the parking reason. Park

Data: workflow return (reviewed[], grade, commentary, ledger_fixes) + wave Paper §Debrief.

Slide 11 — The Debrief & GATE 5: next wave?

Job: close the story, open the next. The wave Paper is now complete — direction → coverage → proofs → decisions → outcome — and this slide is its executive rendering plus the loop-back.

  • what shipped vs what the wish asked (holistic, not a checklist)
  • the next_wave handoff — what the reviewer says the next wave should take, pre-filled as the next wave's draft direction
  • backlog state: open children on the epic, by priority — the future the Decide phase seeded
  • gate: fire the next wave (loops to Slide 2 with the handoff as input) or close the epic

Someone opening the Paper mid-wave must see exactly where the wave stands — the deck is that sentence, made navigable.

The fleet, everywhere: riding the chat surface

The user's explicit ask: see the amount of agents, visualize details realtime, using our chat features. The Studio Claude chat (SESSIONS epic — terminal soul, composer cockpit, agents rail, per-agent drill-down) is the substrate; the deck is a projection over a wave-scoped session. Concretely:

Per wave: total spawned, by model tier. The numbers are the pulse of the whole experience. COUNT

blocks.text: What the strategist found in five minutes

items: **The lockstep is real and green.** `node design/emit.mjs --check` reports **all 17 artifacts in sync** (16 surfaces + paper-editor mirror): cloud SPA, paper-surface, Studio, /papers reader skin, web demo, web TS tokens, Go board, Go pdrender, Go semrole, Go CLI chrome, Elixir render tokens, Elixir Studio categorical, login (session_html), error page (error_html), status page chrome, /sheets reader, paper-editor mirror.

**But the epic ledger says otherwise.** The anchor has **4 acceptance criteria, all `met: false` with empty evidence**, and **23 open children of 55** — including tasks whose own titles say "(SHIPPED)" (`au-w5-paper-components-view`), a full W5.B paper-component-block series (hero, banner, keyvalue, chips, matrix, quote, meter, steps, accordion, sparkline, chart), the W5.D styleguide gallery, W6 brand-mark + visual audit, and one contradiction: `au-w5-pdrender-web-tokens` is open while emit --check lists "Go pdrender: ok".

**The wish's candidate gap surfaces are not in the 17-artifact list by name:** email templates (GUI-premium epic shipped 14 email types — through the manifest or past it?), the /activate control-plane page, any marketing/docs site, PDF/print. These need verification, not assumption.

content.value: **This is a RECONCILIATION wave, not a build wave.** The system is alive and governing; the ledger is stale. The finished experience: the epic anchor either closed with every criterion stamped `met: true` + file:line + PR evidence, or carrying exactly the honest remainder — and nothing in between.
Three streams, in lean order:

items: **Evidence the 4 anchor criteria.** Each criterion gets concrete file:line + PR/CI proof (manifest single-source, four surface-families adopted, drift gate green in CI, styleguides ratified). If any criterion cannot be evidenced, that IS the wave's work.

**Triage the 23 open children into three bins:** (i) *shipped elsewhere* — close with evidence pointing at the PR that shipped it (the PortableDoc showcase, TUI creative slates, and studio-ui-premium epics plausibly absorbed much of W5.B); (ii) *obsolete/superseded* — close as cut with one-line rationale; (iii) *genuinely open* — keep, and decide whether it blocks epic-close or moves to a small named successor task (the epic must not stay open as a component-block wishlist).

**Verify the outside-candidates.** Email, /activate CP page, marketing/docs site, PDF/print: for each, either prove it draws from the lockstep (or is out of the anchor's scope with a written rationale) or cut ONE smallest slice through the same manifest. Suspected true gaps: **email** (not in the 17-artifact list) and possibly `--color-graph-canvas` (open child `au-w3-graph-canvas-token`).

content.value: **Leaning:** (a)-with-a-small-(b) — stamp and close the anchor this wave, with at most 1-3 surgical build slices (email tokens, graph-canvas token, pdrender-open-task reconciliation) if the verifiers prove real gaps. Tree-tidiness earns nothing; honest evidence earns everything.

The lockstep is proven green, twice over.** `node design/emit.mjs --check` = all 17 artifacts in sync; `node design/check.mjs` = Parts A–H PASS (Part F theme-compiler byte-identity, Part H 162/162 WCAG-AA), run live by two independent surveyors AND confirmed in the real CI log (doc-gates run 29128797161 on HEAD 91531b27). **2. The wish's four candidate gap surfaces mostly dissolved on contact:**

items: **Email — NOT a gap.** The "14 GUI-premium email types" are the 14 PortableDoc fleet block types rendered `:email` for the mailed-paper view, and they draw through `Palettes.email_skin → TokensGen` = artifact #11/17 (`api/lib/barkpark/portable_doc/render/tokens_gen.ex`, generated from tokens.json `paperEmail`). Transactional emails (reset/invite/digest) are plain text — no aesthetic surface at all.

**/activate + CP login — NOT a gap.** All CP routes (`/`, `/dashboard`, `/new`, `/activate`) serve one SPA (`router.ex:317-348` → `index.html:14` → `app.css`), and `app.css` IS the "cloud SPA" lockstep artifact (emit.mjs:1720). Login/signup are JS modes of the same screen.

**Marketing/docs site — scope-cut.** barkpark.cloud is served by web/ (in lockstep as "web demo" + "web TS tokens"). `js/docs/` (Fumadocs) is genuinely outside the lockstep but is a known-dormant, unwired, undeployed app — pre-existing decision record at `docs/decisions/deferred.md:8`. Tokenizing an unserved site earns nothing.

**PDF/print — scope-cut.** No PDF pipeline exists anywhere (repo-wide grep clean). Print = tokenized `@media print` blocks in both reader layouts (`sheets.html.heex:261-277`, `bulldocs.html.heex:838-878`) with exactly one frozen paper-white literal each (exemptions.json:13, PR #2273).

# Aesthetic Unification — Reconciliation Wave of 2026-07-11

**Epic anchor:** `aesthetic-unification-epic` — "Apply the cloud design profile to every Barkpark surface" (priority 1, open).
**Wave status: COMPLETE (2026-07-11)** — all 3 slices built, reviewed grade A-; see the DEBRIEF at the bottom. This Paper is the wave's full story: Digest, Decide, and Review each appended below.

## The wish

Decide honestly whether the anchor's words are fully evidenced:

- **(a)** if "every Barkpark surface" is covered by the shipped 17-artifact lockstep (web reader, Studio, email, TUI, CLI chrome, cloud console, error pages…), stamp the anchor's criteria with file:line + PR evidence and **CLOSE the epic**;
- **(b)** if a surface is genuinely OUTSIDE the lockstep (verify, don't assume: docs-site, web demo app, /activate+login CP pages, barkpark.cloud marketing, PDF/print), cut the **smallest honest wave** to bring it through the SAME manifest — never a parallel token system.

Hard constraints: tokens only via the 3-file lockstep (`design/tokens.json` + `derive.mjs` + `emit.mjs`); `check.mjs` stays green incl. Part F byte-identity and Part H AA; studio-literal-check zero new lit-allows; .ex/.heex waits for Elixir Test; worktrees from origin/main; builders claim first; PR bodies carry `Task: <id>`.

## What the strategist found in five minutes

1. **The lockstep is real and green.** `node design/emit.mjs --check` reports **all 17 artifacts in sync** (16 surfaces + paper-editor mirror): cloud SPA, paper-surface, Studio, /papers reader skin, web demo, web TS tokens, Go board, Go pdrender, Go semrole, Go CLI chrome, Elixir render tokens, Elixir Studio categorical, login (session_html), error page (error_html), status page chrome, /sheets reader, paper-editor mirror.
2. **But the epic ledger says otherwise.** The anchor has **4 acceptance criteria, all `met: false` with empty evidence**, and **23 open children of 55** — including tasks whose own titles say "(SHIPPED)" (`au-w5-paper-components-view`), a full W5.B paper-component-block series (hero, banner, keyvalue, chips, matrix, quote, meter, steps, accordion, sparkline, chart), the W5.D styleguide gallery, W6 brand-mark + visual audit, and one contradiction: `au-w5-pdrender-web-tokens` is open while emit --check lists "Go pdrender: ok".
3. **The wish's candidate gap surfaces are not in the 17-artifact list by name:** email templates (GUI-premium epic shipped 14 email types — through the manifest or past it?), the /activate control-plane page, any marketing/docs site, PDF/print. These need verification, not assumption.

## Strategic direction (tentative — Decide finalizes)

**This is a RECONCILIATION wave, not a build wave.** The system is alive and governing; the ledger is stale. The finished experience: the epic anchor either closed with every criterion stamped `met: true` + file:line + PR evidence, or carrying exactly the honest remainder — and nothing in between.

Three streams, in lean order:

1. **Evidence the 4 anchor criteria.** Each criterion gets concrete file:line + PR/CI proof (manifest single-source, four surface-families adopted, drift gate green in CI, styleguides ratified). If any criterion cannot be evidenced, that IS the wave's work.
2. **Triage the 23 open children into three bins:** (i) *shipped elsewhere* — close with evidence pointing at the PR that shipped it (the PortableDoc showcase, TUI creative slates, and studio-ui-premium epics plausibly absorbed much of W5.B); (ii) *obsolete/superseded* — close as cut with one-line rationale; (iii) *genuinely open* — keep, and decide whether it blocks epic-close or moves to a small named successor task (the epic must not stay open as a component-block wishlist).
3. **Verify the outside-candidates.** Email, /activate CP page, marketing/docs site, PDF/print: for each, either prove it draws from the lockstep (or is out of the anchor's scope with a written rationale) or cut ONE smallest slice through the same manifest. Suspected true gaps: **email** (not in the 17-artifact list) and possibly `--color-graph-canvas` (open child `au-w3-graph-canvas-token`).

**Leaning:** (a)-with-a-small-(b) — stamp and close the anchor this wave, with at most 1-3 surgical build slices (email tokens, graph-canvas token, pdrender-open-task reconciliation) if the verifiers prove real gaps. Tree-tidiness earns nothing; honest evidence earns everything.

*Reviewer (Fable), last hands before merge. Reviewed all 3 green slices end-to-end, fixed one cross-slice break in place, re-ran every gate on the true integrated tree. **Grade: A-.***

What shipped (per slice, integration-ordered core → sweep → editor)

**S1 — `ae-upsert-paper-wall` (core).** Final branch `loop-epic/seal-the-last-wall-bypass-authoringwall--0-r`. `Barkpark.Content.AuthoringWall.enforce/5` is now the ONE shared chain: exemption-read-once → label spine → E3 registry → E4 dedup → clear-on-FULL-pass → main_tag stamp. `Lifecycle.publish_document` delegates byte-identically (its 225-line inline chain is gone). `BlockOps.upsert_paper` mounts the same chain on a synthesized `%Document{}` ref (doc_id = slug) BEFORE the Repo write — the self-id reaches DedupWall's incumbent exclusion so a paper can never near-duplicate itself. The single ingest-referencing file not touched (`capabilities_project_test`) is a capability-tier visibility test, not a paper birth. No uncovered wall-facing path remains.

**S3 — `ae-editor-legacy-tag-writeloss`.** Final branch `loop-epic/paperfieldblock-composite-editor-must-no-2-r` (= core + editor + reviewer fix). Two seams: a RENDER seam (`normalize_legacy_composite_rows`, SCOPED to composites that declare a `"tag"` subfield) reconstitutes a legacy bare-string row to `%{"tag"=>s}` before the editor renders it; plus the charter-mandated generic `ensure_map` `is_binary` merge head as belt-and-suspenders. The protective test reds without the fix and greens with it; two genericity-guard tests pin a non-tag composite (amount/currency) and a scalar arrayOf (keywords) round-tripping unharmed with NO spurious `tag` key. **Directory gate 103/0 on the integration.**

What the reviewer fixed in place (the one real blemish)

The editor slice was filed "independent, parallel-safe" — it is NOT. Its seed helpers, and the shared `PaperEditorTestHelpers` it `use`s (which the sweep wrapped), birth papers through bare `upsert_paper` with no tags. The merged wall 422s those births. Cross-slice reality the lead MUST honor

These are ONE integrated unit, not three independent merges. Because D35 split the mount (breaks ~288 fixtures) from the sweep (repairs them), **a core-only PR REDS the full Elixir Test gate.** Merge order MUST be core → sweep → editor, stacked. All three -r branches carry the single core commit (git dedupes on merge); the slice file sets are disjoint; the full gate is green only on the combined tip. The editor slice depends on BOTH core (for `bypass_wall/2` to compile) AND sweep (for the shared helper wrap). Ledger audit

Honest across all three tasks: each `in_progress`, every built criterion stamped `met` with evidence as the work happened, the merge-gated criterion left `met=false` for the lead to close on merge. No lies or omissions to correct. The reviewer's editor-seed fix is recorded here and in the charter wave log, not as a criterion flip.

Grade: A-

The wave FINISHES the epic's central promise — one fail-closed door for every published paper and task, the last bypass sealed — with high correctness and PROVEN completeness (the sweep's coverage is a set-difference, not a claim), and it REDUCES duplication (a shared chokepoint replaces two forked chains). The single deduction is the editor slice's vacuous green: its gate passed pre-integration and would have reddened the merge, requiring reviewer intervention to catch — exactly the distrust-vacuous-green lesson the charter carries. The delivered, fixed, integrated result is excellent.

*Status: COMPLETE. The wall is mounted at all FIVE seams. Remaining epic work is backlog observability + doc-truth (see the charter wave log), none blocking the north star.*

---

## What actually landed vs the ledger (reconciliation — read this first)

Two ledger claims did not survive contact with `main`. The wave is shaped by fixing them honestly.

**FINDING 1 — D28 is NOT on main (false-done).** The ledger marks `ae-w4-ratchet-telemetry` **done (6/6)** and the charter wave-2 review cites #2817 as merged. But:

- `git merge-base --is-ancestor d343c793 HEAD` → **NOT in main**. Commit #2817 exists, but lives only on unrelated branches (`loop-epic/…chat…`, `omx/task…`) — it was **never merged to main**.

**The silver lining:** the preserved worktree's `authoring_wall.ex` **already folds the fixed D28 semantics into the extraction** — its `enforce/5` clears the exemption only on a full pass (`if exempt? and spine_passed?`) and `stamp_main_tag/2` is recompute-else-drop. **FINDING 2 — `ae-caller-error-surfacing` (D23) IS on main (the lead's note is stale).** #2793 (`900981af`) merged; `adopt.ex` carries the `collapse` field + `{:ok, doc, collapse}`, `link.ex` logs, valueref gained the `publish_failed` clause, Studio drains advisories. **FINDING 3 — the worktree is 100 commits behind main and its diff is contaminated.** `git diff main --stat` from the worktree shows deletions of `bp-chat-tui-charter.md` (−81), `bp-hyperquiz-charter.md` (−53), `listen_controller.ex` (−85), `listen_backpressure_test.exs` (−174), `chat_transcript_window_test.exs` (−99), `rate_limit_test.exs`. **These are not extraction work** — they are reversions of post-fork main work the stale base never saw. content.value: *Living wave paper. Opened at Strategize (2026-07-13). Every later phase appends here — Digest folds the survey, Decide records the wave plan, Review closes the story. Workers never write this paper; they write their own bp task.*

Epic: `authoring-excellence` · Charter: `.claude/workflows/bp-authoring-excellence-charter.md` (authoritative over the design paper). Prior waves: wave-2026-07-10 (wall built), -07-12 (D10 window closed, search payoff), -07-12b (feedback rings), -07-13 (last bypass extracted). This wave (07-13b): **make the extraction's full-suite gate actually green.**

Wave 4 built the flagship: one shared `Barkpark.Content.AuthoringWall.enforce/5` — a single fail-closed door for every published paper AND task, whether born through `lifecycle.publish_document` or `BlockOps.upsert_paper`. PR #2881 (branch `loop-epic/ae-w4-seal-last-bypass-integrated`) carries the extraction + a 114-callsite fixture sweep + the editor legacy-tag fix. The wave-4 review stamped it "SEALED, grade A-".

But that green was **directory-scoped** (content+papers 829/0, web-controllers+studio 2154/1) — NOT the full suite. `CC=/usr/bin/clang mix test` is **RED with 6 failures**, all one class: an untagged PAPER publish returns 422 `label_spine`. These ~5 flows publish papers via HTTP mutate / LiveView / a projection seam — NOT the swept `upsert_paper(attrs)` helper — so the fixture sweep never touched them. The wall works exactly as designed; the fixtures never learned to carry tags on these paths.

FINISH and LAND the held wall. Resume from `loop-epic/ae-w4-seal-last-bypass-integrated` (rebase on current origin/main — 2 commits ahead: #2883 mutate double-nesting warn, #2882 portabledoc reader). Make the 6 flows pass by registering weighted tags in each flow's setup (`LabelFixtures.register_tags!`) + adding them to the paper mutate/LiveView payload — the SAME tag-spine the fixture-sweep applied, extended to the API/LiveView paper-creation paths. Fail-before / pass-after per flow. Then `CC=/usr/bin/clang mix test` must be FULLY green (the co-dependency check). Do NOT touch the wall's type scope (`@walled_types ~w(paper task)`; sheets/posts unwalled). Do NOT re-extract the wall. Do NOT reopen `ae-w4-ratchet-telemetry` (#2817 correctly landed). Also fold in D36 `ae-ingest-advisory-deadletter` if tractable as a SEPARATE opus slice.

items: `api/test/barkpark/sheets_m0_proof_test.exs` — publishes via `POST /v1/data/mutate`; the sheet-backed paper projection falls through to `upsert_paper`.
`api/test/barkpark/sheets_m1_proof_test.exs` — **TWO failures**: the M1 write-through story AND the "two colleagues edit the budget live" LiveView collab test.
`api/test/barkpark_web/controllers/bulldocs_email_controller_test.exs` — publishes a paper via the email-controller path.
`api/test/barkpark_web/integration/preview_routes_test.exs` — creates/publishes a paper to exercise preview routes.

content.value: This is a **FINISH wave**, not a design wave. The wall is correct and must not move. The disciplined outcome: the full suite goes green because EACH failing flow carries a registered, weighted tag on its paper-publish payload — the exact tag-spine the sweep applied, now reaching the HTTP-mutate / LiveView / projection birth paths the sweep couldn't see. Fail-before/pass-after evidence per flow; then the whole `CC=/usr/bin/clang mix test` green as the co-dependency proof.

**THE ONE QUESTION THAT DECIDES THE FIX SHAPE** (survey must resolve it): are these TEST-ONLY fixture gaps, or do they expose an UNAUDITED PRODUCTION paper-birth path? If a real sheet publish, a real email-controller publish, or a real preview generation projects an untagged paper in prod, the honest fix is **product code** (the projection seam threads synthesized tags OR carries an explicit `bypass_wall: true` + rationale, exactly as D26 audited the lib callers) — and the test merely proves it. If they are pure fixtures birthing test papers, the wish's "register tags in setup + payload" is right and the change is test-only.

I LEAN toward **honest per-flow classification**: genuinely-authored publishes (email, collab budget doc) carry tags; machine PROJECTIONS (sheet view, preview render) that were never meant to be search-findable carry a product-code bypass with a grep-able rationale — the same doctrine D26 used for plan_papers and seeds. Decide finalizes after two explore rounds.

**Quality bar (Kinsta/Vercel):** a rejected publish must cost an agent ONE retry with a machine-readable error — never a silent 422 on a path a real user hits. So if any of these 6 is a live prod path, shipping test-only tags would leave prod broken. The verify fleet must check prod reality, not just the test tree.

Fable EXHAUSTED. Every `builder_model = opus`; decompose too-hard slices into smaller opus slices; NEVER Haiku. Verify fleet: opus for correctness digs, sonnet only for breadth mapping. Primary slice resumes the held branch, rebases on origin/main, fixes ONLY the ~5 non-fixture paper-publish flows, proves full green. Optional second opus slice: D36 `ae-ingest-advisory-deadletter` — but it COLLIDES with the primary on `bulldocs_ingest_controller.ex`, so sequence it, don't parallelize. Main checkout stays on main; all builds in isolated worktrees; gate Elixir in the integration worktree (build-borrow-broken). `.ex/.exs/.heex` WAIT for the Elixir Test gate before merge.

14 broad Sonnet surveyors are mapping each failing flow's exact paper-publish seam, whether it is test-only or a real prod path, the `LabelFixtures` API surface for extending to payloads, the wave-4 `bypass_wall` audit gaps, the full-suite gate co-dependency, the rebase delta, and D36 tractability. Digest distills the reports into the verify plan; Decide rules the per-flow fix shape (tags vs product bypass) before builders fly.

*Living wave paper. Opened at Strategize (2026-07-13). Every later phase appends here — Digest folds the survey, Decide records the wave plan, Review closes the story. Workers never write this paper; they write their own bp task.*

Epic: `authoring-excellence` · Charter: `.claude/workflows/bp-authoring-excellence-charter.md` (authoritative over the design paper). This wave (07-13b): **make the extraction's full-suite gate actually green.**

The situation

Wave 4 built the flagship: one shared `Barkpark.Content.AuthoringWall.enforce/5` — a single fail-closed door for every published paper AND task, whether born through `lifecycle.publish_document` or `BlockOps.upsert_paper`. PR #2881 (branch `loop-epic/ae-w4-seal-last-bypass-integrated`) carries the extraction + a 114-callsite fixture sweep + the editor legacy-tag fix. The wave-4 review stamped it "SEALED, grade A-".

But that green was **directory-scoped** (content+papers 829/0, web-controllers+studio 2154/1) — NOT the full suite. `CC=/usr/bin/clang mix test` is **RED with 6 failures**, all one class: an untagged PAPER publish returns 422 `label_spine`. These ~5 flows publish papers via HTTP mutate / LiveView / a projection seam — NOT the swept `upsert_paper(attrs)` helper — so the fixture sweep never touched them. The wall works exactly as designed; the fixtures never learned to carry tags on these paths.

The wish (verbatim intent)

FINISH and LAND the held wall. Resume from `loop-epic/ae-w4-seal-last-bypass-integrated` (rebase on current origin/main — 2 commits ahead: #2883 mutate double-nesting warn, #2882 portabledoc reader). Make the 6 flows pass by registering weighted tags in each flow's setup (`LabelFixtures.register_tags!`) + adding them to the paper mutate/LiveView payload — the SAME tag-spine the fixture-sweep applied, extended to the API/LiveView paper-creation paths. Fail-before / pass-after per flow. Then `CC=/usr/bin/clang mix test` must be FULLY green (the co-dependency check). Do NOT touch the wall's type scope (`@walled_types ~w(paper task)`; sheets/posts unwalled). Do NOT re-extract the wall. Do NOT reopen `ae-w4-ratchet-telemetry` (#2817 correctly landed). Also fold in D36 `ae-ingest-advisory-deadletter` if tractable as a SEPARATE opus slice.

The 6 failing flows (5 files)

  • `api/test/barkpark/sheets_m0_proof_test.exs` — publishes via `POST /v1/data/mutate`; the sheet-backed paper projection falls through to `upsert_paper`.
  • `api/test/barkpark/sheets_m1_proof_test.exs` — **TWO failures**: the M1 write-through story AND the "two colleagues edit the budget live" LiveView collab test.
  • `api/test/barkpark_web/controllers/bulldocs_email_controller_test.exs` — publishes a paper via the email-controller path.
  • `api/test/barkpark_web/integration/preview_routes_test.exs` — creates/publishes a paper to exercise preview routes.

Strategic direction

This is a **FINISH wave**, not a design wave. The wall is correct and must not move. The disciplined outcome: the full suite goes green because EACH failing flow carries a registered, weighted tag on its paper-publish payload — the exact tag-spine the sweep applied, now reaching the HTTP-mutate / LiveView / projection birth paths the sweep couldn't see. Fail-before/pass-after evidence per flow; then the whole `CC=/usr/bin/clang mix test` green as the co-dependency proof.

**THE ONE QUESTION THAT DECIDES THE FIX SHAPE** (survey must resolve it): are these TEST-ONLY fixture gaps, or do they expose an UNAUDITED PRODUCTION paper-birth path? If a real sheet publish, a real email-controller publish, or a real preview generation projects an untagged paper in prod, the honest fix is **product code** (the projection seam threads synthesized tags OR carries an explicit `bypass_wall: true` + rationale, exactly as D26 audited the lib callers) — and the test merely proves it. If they are pure fixtures birthing test papers, the wish's "register tags in setup + payload" is right and the change is test-only.

I LEAN toward **honest per-flow classification**: genuinely-authored publishes (email, collab budget doc) carry tags; machine PROJECTIONS (sheet view, preview render) that were never meant to be search-findable carry a product-code bypass with a grep-able rationale — the same doctrine D26 used for plan_papers and seeds. Decide finalizes after two explore rounds.

**Quality bar (Kinsta/Vercel):** a rejected publish must cost an agent ONE retry with a machine-readable error — never a silent 422 on a path a real user hits. So if any of these 6 is a live prod path, shipping test-only tags would leave prod broken. The verify fleet must check prod reality, not just the test tree.

Model constraint & shape

14 broad Sonnet surveyors are mapping each failing flow's exact paper-publish seam, whether it is test-only or a real prod path, the `LabelFixtures` API surface for extending to payloads, the wave-4 `bypass_wall` audit gaps, the full-suite gate co-dependency, the rebase delta, and D36 tractability. What the next wave takes

Backlog only — the wall is complete. `ae-paper-decision-sync` (WIDENED: full D18–D42 table regen, all design-paper anchors stale), `ae-curator-feed` (persisted findings, deferred until a consumer exists), `ae-dedup-trgm-index` (rewrite DedupWall `similarity()>0.1` to the `%` operator before any type holds thousands of published docs), `ae-w4-findability-posttest` (D9 Oban self-query — filed, unbuilt), `ae-search-eval-baseline-repair`, `ae-boot-gate-ci`, `ae-js-sdk-strength-filter`, and `ae-preview-routes-pollution-guard` (harden the `async:false` `Application.put_env(:barkpark,:preview,…)` cross-test pollution the full-suite flakes exposed).
